title: Reasoning and Logic
summary: The grade rests on one closed-book written endterm of 180 minutes, with a resit. A 120-minute midterm in week 5 and the Prolog project can only add a bonus. Every paper is all open questions in a fixed order that follows the course, from a truth table to a closing logic puzzle. Proofs and constructions together carry about half of the points.

basis.note: The archive lists 13 more papers. Seven of them (2022 and 2023 midterm, endterm and resit, and MCQ Test 2023) were read for trends only; the 2020 and 2021 papers had no text. Papers carry the academic year on the cover (2024-25 is the 2025 set). Shares use printed points over 347 points, sub-question by sub-question; invariant problems count under induction.

format.mode: Written, closed-book exam on paper, with open questions only
format.duration: Endterm and resit 180 minutes; midterm 120 minutes
format.structure: Endterms and resits have 14 to 16 questions worth 60 or 70 points, in course order: a truth table, true-or-false claims, translations both ways, a formal structure, proof techniques in an excerpt, a number proof, induction, an invariant problem, recursive sets, sets, relations and functions, TREE functions and a puzzle. Midterms have 10 questions worth 40 to 55 points on chapters 1 to 3.
format.grading: The endterm grade F is the base. Midterm M and project P give a bonus B = min(10, max(0, 2 x floor(M - 5)) + max(0, 2 x floor(P - 5))), and the course grade is F + B(10 - F)/100. A resit replaces F with the same bonus and the higher result counts. Each paper is graded as 1 + 9 x score / total.
format.aids: None: no book, notes or calculator. Bring a pen and your campus card.

topicWeights.asks: Always question 1: a full truth table, often for a new operator defined by its own table, then validity or equivalence with reference to rows, or a DNF. Also true-or-false claims about arguments, explosion and satisfiability, and converses in English.

Two or three English sentences into logic and two or three formulas back into English, a negation to simplify, and a Tarski world or formal structure with a bounded domain that satisfies statements or breaks an argument.
A 4 to 6-point proof of a claim about integers, usually by division into cases or contradiction, plus a 2-point excerpt from a real paper or course in which you name the two techniques used.

An induction proof of a sum, divisibility or recurrence; describing the base case and step for a restricted claim; computing or writing a recursive sequence; and on endterms a 4 to 5-point invariant proof for a game or process.
On every endterm and resit: write a recursive definition for a described set of words or numbers (3 points), then prove a property of all its elements by structural induction (4 to 6 points).

Draw a binary tree with set leaves and traversal sequence, evaluate a given TREE function on a drawn tree, write your own TREE function, and draw a directed graph or DAG with constraints on its topological orderings.
Small endterm items: list a product or power set, draw a Venn diagram, or prove or disprove a claim about all sets.
Check reflexive, symmetric, transitive or antisymmetric for a given relation, build a relation with given properties, judge injective or surjective, and argue that a set is countable.
A closing 3-point story puzzle about the coati kingdom: reconstruct a score table, a team assignment, a safe code or the last move of a game, explaining every elimination.

questionTypes.description: A full written proof: cases, contradiction or contrapositive, mathematical or structural induction, or a four-part invariant proof.
Build an object that meets given conditions: a Tarski world, formal structure, tree, graph, relation, recursive definition or recursive function on TREE.
Fill in truth tables, rewrite to DNF or CNF, negate formulas, evaluate recursive functions, or list power sets and products.
Turn English into predicate logic with your own predicates and constants, or formulas into natural English.
Name proof techniques in an excerpt, say what a base case and step must show, or give an informal argument such as countability.
Decide whether a general claim holds and justify it, giving a concrete counterexample when it fails.
A story puzzle solved by elimination, marked on the written reasoning, not only the answer.

recurring: Question 1 is always a truth table of 5 to 9 points, in five of the six papers for a made-up operator defined by its own table.
Every paper has a 2-point question with an excerpt from a research paper or another course's proof (Wiles, Algorithm Design): name the two techniques used and cite the lines.
Translations go both ways in every paper; endterms add sets, functions and cardinality such as "more books than students".
A Tarski world or formal structure with a bounded domain size appears in every paper.
Number proofs [[forbid modular arithmetic]] but let you write n as kx + r, so division into cases by remainder is the expected route.
Since 2024 every endterm and resit has a 4 to 5-point invariant proof about a game or a mixing process, marked on initialisation, iteration, eventual falsity and post-condition.
Endterms and resits always pair a TREE function to evaluate with one you must write yourself.
Every paper ends with a 3-point coati-kingdom puzzle, and the story continues from one paper to the next.
trends: Endterms grew from 57 points in 2022 to 69 and 70 points in 2023 and 2024, then dropped to 60 points in 2025; midterms shrank from 54 and 55 to 47 and then 40 points.
A 20-question multiple-choice test on modules 1 and 2 ran alongside the midterm in the 2023 set; there is no multiple choice since.
Countability came back in Resit 2024 and both 2025 papers as a bijection or an informal argument, and Endterm 2025 added a partial-order check.
strategy: Make question 1 safe: practise 8-row tables in a fixed row order, new operators read from a table, and a DNF taken from the true rows.
Learn the proof templates exactly as the rubrics score them: [[base case, hypothesis for an arbitrary k, use of the hypothesis, conclusion]]; for invariants the four parts.
Work through the 2024 and 2025 papers against the clock; the question order hardly changes, so you can plan minutes per block.
For predicate logic, write out your predicates and constants first and reread your English translation aloud: it must sound like normal English.
For TREE functions write the empty-tree and leaf cases first, then sum over the children; check your function on the example tree in the question.
Answer exactly what is asked: start with True or False or Yes or No when told to, and leave out side remarks, since irrelevant information can cost points.
Leave the closing puzzle for last unless you are quick at it, but write down each elimination: partial reasoning scores.
pitfalls: Assuming the claim: "take an arbitrary k such that the claim holds" in a direct proof, or the full claim as induction hypothesis, both lose points.
A contradiction proof must start from [["there exists" a counterexample]], not from an arbitrary element.
Translations into English that keep "there exists an x such that" are marked wrong.
Tarski worlds lose a point each for a domain size outside the bounds, unshaped objects or duplicate names.
Relation questions: swapping two property names costs a point, and each failing property needs its own counterexample.
Recursive definitions lose points for a missing exclusion rule or inconsistent notation, such as braces where tuples need round brackets.
